title: How to Balance EE Research With Everything Else
summary: Learn how to balance EE research with classes, IAs, CAS and tests using a realistic September-November schedule built around focused weekly progress.
body_markdown:
The September-November term is difficult because Extended Essay research competes with tests, IAs, TOK, CAS and ordinary homework. To **balance EE research with everything else** , protect a few weekly sessions, define a concrete output for each one and plan backward from your school's internal deadlines.


You do not need to work on the EE every day. You need a reliable system that prevents long gaps while preserving time for subject learning, sleep and other Diploma Programme requirements.


### Know which deadlines apply


The[IB describes the Extended Essay](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/extended-essay/what-is-the-extended-essay/) as an independent research project culminating in a paper of up to **4,000 words** . Students complete **three mandatory reflection sessions** with their supervisor, with the final session called the **viva voce** .


The IB sets submission dates for schools, but your coordinator determines the internal deadlines you follow. These may cover the proposal, research question, outline, reflections and draft. A timeline from another school is therefore not authoritative for your situation.


The assessment model has been revised for **first assessment in May 2027** . Students working during 2026-2027 should confirm their assessment session and criteria with their coordinator. The[official IB Extended Essay update](https://ibo.org/university-admission/latest-curriculum-updates/dp-extended-essay-updates/) outlines the revised framework.


Record these dates in one calendar:


- EE proposal, outline and draft deadlines
- Supervisor and reflection meetings
- IA and TOK deadlines
- Tests and examinations
- CAS and personal commitments


### Choose a measurable November outcome


Avoid goals such as "finish my research." Research has no natural endpoint, so this wording encourages endless reading. Set an outcome that produces evidence of progress.


A realistic November target might include:


- A focused, feasible **research question**
- Credible sources or usable primary data
- Notes linked to claims and citations
- A provisional answer or thesis
- An argument-led outline
- One analytical section, if required by your school


This is practical advice, not a universal IB calendar. A student whose draft is due in November must move faster than someone still testing topic feasibility. Begin with your actual school deadline and work backward.


### Use an 11-week fall-term plan


This schedule gives the **IB EE fall term** a logical progression without allowing the essay to dominate every week.


Period EE priority Concrete output


September, weeks 1-2 Confirm subject fit and scope Two or three possible questions and a source-access check


September, weeks 3-4 Begin preliminary research Working question, method note and source log


October, weeks 1-2 Deepen research Evidence notes with citations and limitations


October, weeks 3-4 Test the argument Provisional answer, counterargument and section plan


November, weeks 1-2 Fill evidence gaps Targeted research for unsupported claims


November, weeks 3-4 Consolidate progress Updated outline, drafted section and supervisor questions


Treat this plan as adjustable. If essential evidence is unavailable, narrowing the question represents progress. The[RevisionDojo EE research-question guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ee-research-question-what-works-2027) can help you assess whether a question is focused, analytical and feasible within 4,000 words.


### Build a two-lane weekly schedule


Separate your workload into two lanes. The **deadline lane** contains tests, homework and coursework due soon. The **continuity lane** contains long-term work, including the EE, that becomes urgent when neglected.


A sustainable week could contain:


- **Two 45-minute EE blocks** for analysis, data processing or outlining
- **One 15-minute maintenance block** for citations and file organization
- Subject revision arranged around upcoming tests
- One buffer period for unexpected work
- A 10-minute weekly planning review


Never schedule only "work on EE." Use a specific action such as "evaluate two articles for claim 2" or "convert notes into three outline points." A defined finish line makes a short session productive.


During a heavy test week, retain only one research block or the maintenance session. During a lighter week, add a 90-minute block. Balance means varying the workload deliberately, not dividing every week equally.


### Make every research session produce something


Reading can feel productive while leaving nothing usable. Each session should create an **artifact** , such as a source entry, evidence table, graph, paragraph plan, method decision or revised question.


For each source, record:


- Full citation details and page numbers
- Its central claim or evidence
- Its relevance to your research question
- Authority, method and limitations
- Agreements or conflicts with other evidence
- The section where you may use it


The[RevisionDojo guide to EE sources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-are-the-best-sources-for-ib-extended-essay-research) explains how to screen evidence. Recording citations immediately also prevents the difficult task of reconstructing references near submission.


By November, search for evidence that fills a named gap instead of collecting broadly relevant material. If you cannot explain what a source contributes to your argument, it may not deserve more time.


### Protect grades and use your supervisor well


Do not abandon routine subject practice because the EE feels urgent. Tests require repeated retrieval, while EE research usually advances through fewer, deeper sessions. Short active-recall and exam-question blocks can preserve subject progress; RevisionDojo's[Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/questionbank) can make this practice more focused.


Reserve your strongest concentration period for the week's hardest task. That might be an EE method decision on Tuesday and mathematics revision on Thursday. Set a stopping time because a plan dependent on repeated late nights will reduce the quality of both research and classroom learning.


Your supervisor guides the process, but you remain responsible for the work. Bring evidence of progress and focused questions about scope, methodology, source quality or overly descriptive sections.


Keep brief dated notes in a **Researcher's Reflection Space** . This supports reflection but is not itself the final assessed submission. RevisionDojo's[RRS explanation](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ee-rrs-researchers-reflection-space) shows how to record decisions, obstacles and changes efficiently.


### Recover quickly when plans slip


Do not attempt to repay every missed hour in one weekend. Check the next deadline, identify the smallest useful output and schedule one 25-45 minute restart block within 48 hours. Tell your supervisor early if access, scope or methodology is blocking progress.


Avoid false progress such as redesigning documents, searching without reading or repeatedly changing the question without new evidence.[Jojo AI and RevisionDojo's EE support](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-extended-essay-help) can help you test scope or interpret feedback, but they should not replace your reasoning, supervisor or genuine writing.


### Conclusion


To balance EE research with everything else, choose a measurable November outcome, protect two focused blocks in most weeks and maintain accurate source and reflection records. Adjust the workload around genuine deadlines rather than abandoning the essay or sacrificing every free hour.


RevisionDojo's[Extended Essay guides](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ee-guides) , Jojo AI and Coursework Review can support this structure. Use them to plan, clarify questions and review work that you have genuinely produced.
